planting.note: Plant rooted stolon pieces or potted starts at a pond margin in saturated mud or in up to 2 inches of standing water; the creeping stems root at each node, so even a small division will knit into a spreading mat within a season once water temperatures stay above 60°F.

directions: Grow along the shallow, muddy edge of a pond, bog garden, or water feature in full sun to light shade, where the round, peltate leaves and tiny umbels of greenish-white flowers form a low, spreading groundcover over the waterline. This Gulf Coast native spreads quickly by creeping, rooting stolons, knitting together bare mud to reduce erosion and shading out algae at the pond's edge, while its dense mats give cover to small frogs and aquatic insects and its flowers draw tiny native bees and flies. It tolerates both standing water and periods of exposed mud, making it forgiving for beginner water gardeners, and excess growth is simply pulled or trimmed back since it roots shallowly and lifts away easily. Divide and replant clumps anytime during the growing season to fill in new areas of a pond margin.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Center for Aquatic and Invasive Plants

planting.note: Direct sow seed onto exposed mud or press into saturated soil at a marsh or pond margin after the last frost; seed needs light and consistently wet soil to germinate, so avoid burying it. Transplants can also be set into shallow mud through late spring.

directions: Plant at the saturated margin of a pond, ditch, or marsh garden in full sun, where smooth beggarticks produces showy, inch-wide golden-yellow daisy flowers from late summer into fall on smooth, hairless stems distinct from its bristly upland cousins. It is a favorite late-season nectar source for bees and butterflies when little else is blooming near the water, and the flattened, barbed seeds that follow are readily eaten by dabbling ducks and other waterfowl, giving rise to the 'beggarticks' name from how they hitch a ride on feathers and fur. It self-sows readily in bare, damp mud, so it works well for naturalizing a new pond edge, and stray seedlings are easy to thin or transplant. Allow some seed heads to mature and disperse each fall to keep a colony going year to year.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Center for Aquatic and Invasive Plants

planting.note: Anchor rooted crowns or potted divisions in a container of heavy aquatic soil topped with pea gravel and submerge in 6-18 inches of still or slow-moving water; the finely divided underwater leaves establish fastest in cool spring water before summer heat sets in.

directions: Grow fully or partly submerged in a still pond, ditch, or slow backwater in full sun to light shade, where finely dissected, fan-shaped underwater foliage gives way to simpler floating or emergent leaves and bright buttercup-yellow flowers held just above the surface in spring and early summer. This widespread native oxygenates the water column and offers cover for tadpoles, small fish, and aquatic invertebrates, while its early flowers provide nectar for the first native bees active around the pond each season. It spreads gently by creeping stems and can be divided every couple of years to control size or share with another water garden. Note that like most buttercups the foliage and sap are mildly toxic if grazed in quantity, so it is best kept out of stock ponds.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Center for Aquatic and Invasive Plants

planting.note: Set divisions or nursery starts into saturated soil at the brackish or freshwater margin of a pond or marsh garden; the fibrous-rooted rosettes establish quickly in consistently moist to wet ground and tolerate light salt spray near coastal water features.

directions: Plant in saturated soil or shallow water at the edge of a marsh garden, brackish pond, or coastal rain garden in full sun to partial shade, where rosettes of glossy, spoon-shaped leaves send up slender stalks of tiny white, star-shaped flowers through summer. Seaside brookweed is unusually salt-tolerant for a native perennial, making it valuable for gardeners restoring tidal or brackish wetland edges along the Gulf Coast where few other flowering natives persist, and its small flowers attract tiny native bees, flies, and other pollinators that specialize in coastal marsh plants. It spreads slowly into loose colonies by short rhizomes and self-sown seedlings, filling gaps in bare wet mud without becoming aggressive. Established plants need little care beyond keeping the soil consistently wet.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Center for Aquatic and Invasive Plants

planting.note: Float or anchor rooted stem cuttings at the surface of a pond or shallow water garden once water has warmed in spring; the trailing stems root readily at each node and knit together quickly, so a contained planting area or floating basket is recommended to manage spread.

directions: Grow on the surface of a pond or slow backwater in full sun, where mats of trailing, reddish stems and rounded leaves produce cheerful five-petaled yellow flowers through summer just above the waterline. This Gulf Coast native forms dense floating mats that give cover and ambush sites for frogs, dragonfly larvae, and small fish, and its flowers are visited by native bees and syrphid flies drawn to the bright yellow blooms. Because it roots at every node and can spread vigorously in nutrient-rich water, it is best grown in a contained basket or a smaller water feature where its coverage can be thinned back by hand rather than in an open natural pond. Regularly pull excess stems in summer to keep open water for fish and other aquatic wildlife.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Center for Aquatic and Invasive Plants

planting.note: Plant rooted stem cuttings or potted divisions in a container of heavy aquatic soil and submerge in 4-12 inches of water at a pond margin; new stems root readily from cuttings pressed directly into soft sediment through the growing season.

directions: Grow submerged or as an emergent marginal in a pond, bog garden, or rain garden basin in full sun to partial shade, where the finely feathered underwater foliage transitions to toothed, bronze-green emergent leaves and inconspicuous flower spikes above the waterline. Mermaid weed is a valuable native oxygenating plant that helps keep pond water clear, and its dense underwater foliage provides essential cover for damselfly and dragonfly nymphs, small fish fry, and other aquatic invertebrates that in turn feed frogs and wading birds. It spreads modestly by creeping, rooting stems along the substrate and is easy to thin by hand if it outgrows its space. Combine with pickerelweed or arrowhead at a pond margin for a fuller native underwater and emergent planting.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Center for Aquatic and Invasive Plants
